title: Joshua 8:1–17
context: With the devoted thing removed and the LORD’s anger turned away (7:26), Joshua 8 tells of the renewed campaign against Ai. This time the LORD speaks first, reassures Joshua with words that echo his commission (1:9), and gives the plan: the whole army goes up, an ambush is set behind the city, and, unlike at Jericho, Israel may keep the livestock and goods as plunder (8:2). Verses 3–17 describe how Joshua sets the ambush between Bethel and Ai and draws the defenders out by a feigned retreat. The narrative contrasts sharply with chapter 7: then human confidence and hidden sin led to defeat; now divine initiative and obedience lead to victory. Some numbers in the account, such as the thirty thousand of 8:3 and the five thousand of 8:12, are explained in different ways by interpreters.

verses.text: The LORD said to Joshua, “Don’t be afraid, and don’t be dismayed. Take all the warriors with you, and arise, go up to Ai. Behold, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, with his people, his city, and his land.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD begins, “Don’t be afraid, and don’t be dismayed,” repeating his words from 1:9 (“Don’t be afraid. Don’t be dismayed”). After the failure of chapter 7, this is a word of restoration. Arminian readers stress the graciousness of God’s renewed promise once sin has been dealt with, and see the command, “Take all the warriors with you,” as calling the whole people into active, trusting obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the initiative now lies wholly with God: “I have given into your hand the king of Ai,” stated in the past tense before the battle begins. The victory is secured by his decree and promise. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God’s gracious restoration after judgment and as a reminder that Israel’s confidence must rest on his word rather than on its own estimate of the enemy.

verses.text: You shall do to Ai and her king as you did to Jericho and her king, except you shall take its goods and its livestock for yourselves. Set an ambush for the city behind it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ai is to be treated as Jericho was, “except you shall take its goods and its livestock for yourselves.” Arminian readers often note the irony: had Achan waited, he could have received plunder lawfully. The verse shows that God’s commands were not meant to deprive his people, and that disobedience grasps for what God may give in his own time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see that the terms of herem are set by God, not by Israel: at Jericho everything was devoted, while at Ai the LORD permits plunder. What is right is what he commands. Shared ground: both traditions read the different instructions as showing that herem was a specific divine command in particular circumstances, and both see the call to trust God’s timing and provision.

verses.text: So Joshua arose, with all the warriors, to go up to Ai. Joshua chose thirty thousand men, the mighty men of valor, and sent them out by night.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua arises “with all the warriors” and chooses “thirty thousand men, the mighty men of valor,” sending them by night. Arminian readers note that, unlike in 7:3, Joshua now follows the LORD’s instructions to involve the whole army. The number differs from the five thousand in 8:12, and interpreters explain this in various ways, such as two separate groups or a different sense for the word for thousand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the obedience to the LORD’s specific command to take all the warriors, a reversal of the overconfidence of the first attack. God works through careful planning and human effort, not apart from them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the obedient start of the renewed campaign, and both acknowledge honestly that the numbers in 8:3 and 8:12 raise questions without a single agreed answer.

verses.text: He commanded them, saying, “Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind the city. Don’t go very far from the city, but all of you be ready.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua commands the ambush to lie “behind the city” and to “be ready.” Arminian readers note that the plan requires disciplined obedience from the soldiers. God’s promise in 8:1 does not make their faithfulness unnecessary; rather, it invites them to act with courage and care within the plan he has given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the detailed instructions as an example of how God’s sovereign promise is fulfilled through ordinary means: strategy, patience and readiness. Trust in God and wise planning are not opposites. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that faith acts, and that God’s people are called to diligence in carrying out what he has commanded.

verses.text: I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. It shall happen, when they come out against us, as at the first, that we will flee before them.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua plans to approach the city and then flee, “as at the first.” The memory of the earlier defeat becomes part of the strategy. Arminian readers observe that God redeems Israel’s failure by turning it into the means of victory, as the defenders of Ai expect a repeat of chapter 7.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God in his providence uses even Israel’s past defeat to accomplish his purposes. What was a humiliation becomes the setting for the enemy’s downfall. Shared ground: both traditions see in the verse a pattern that God can bring good from past failure once sin has been dealt with, without making the failure itself good.

verses.text: They will come out after us until we have drawn them away from the city; for they will say, ‘They flee before us, like the first time.’ So we will flee before them,
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua anticipates the enemy’s words, “They flee before us, like the first time,” and plans to draw them away from the city. Arminian readers note that the defenders of Ai act on their own reasoning and overconfidence, just as Israel did in chapter 7. The reversal is fitting, and those who trusted their own judgment are undone by it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the plan works because God has already given the city into Israel’s hand (8:1), and the enemy’s assumptions serve his purpose. Shared ground: both traditions read the feigned retreat as a legitimate wartime strategy in its setting, and both see the irony that Ai repeats the overconfidence that once cost Israel dearly.

verses.text: and you shall rise up from the ambush, and take possession of the city; for the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The ambush is to rise and take the city, “for the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand.” Arminian readers note that the soldiers’ action and God’s deliverance belong together. The ambush must rise and act, yet the success is credited to the LORD, who works through his people’s obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the confession at the center of the plan: the city falls because the LORD delivers it. Human strategy is real but secondary to divine action. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as holding together human agency and divine deliverance, and neither sees any conflict between them in this narrative.

verses.text: It shall be, when you have seized the city, that you shall set the city on fire. You shall do this according to the LORD’s word. Behold, I have commanded you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The city is to be set on fire “according to the LORD’s word,” and Joshua ends, “Behold, I have commanded you.” Arminian readers note the stress on obedience to God’s word, which runs through the chapter as a contrast to Achan’s disobedience. The soldiers are accountable to carry out exactly what has been commanded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the whole operation is framed by the LORD’s word, which gives it legitimacy and direction. Joshua speaks with authority because he passes on what God has commanded. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the chapter’s emphasis that Israel succeeds when it follows God’s word, in contrast with the failure of chapter 7.

verses.text: Joshua sent them out; and they went to set up the ambush, and stayed between Bethel and Ai on the west side of Ai; but Joshua stayed among the people that night.
verses.arminianNotes: The ambush goes out and stays “between Bethel and Ai on the west side of Ai,” while Joshua remains among the people that night. Arminian readers note Joshua’s presence with the main army as an act of leadership that encourages the people and keeps the plan coordinated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the orderly execution of the plan an example of faithful leadership under God’s direction. Joshua stays where his role requires, trusting the ambush to do its part. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a simple narrative step, showing disciplined obedience and the patient waiting that faith sometimes requires.

verses.text: Joshua rose up early in the morning, mustered the people, and went up, he and the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua again rises “early in the morning,” musters the people, and goes up with the elders “before the people to Ai.” Arminian readers note the leadership of Joshua and the elders, who share responsibility for the outcome, just as they had shared in the mourning of 7:6.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same leaders who humbled themselves before the ark now lead the people into battle. Repentance is followed by renewed service. Shared ground: both traditions see the pattern of humility, obedience and restored leadership as characteristic of God’s dealings with his people after they deal with sin.

verses.text: All the people, even the men of war who were with him, went up and came near, and came before the city and encamped on the north side of Ai. Now there was a valley between him and Ai.
verses.arminianNotes: All the men of war go up and encamp “on the north side of Ai,” with “a valley between him and Ai.” Arminian readers note the openness of the main army’s position, which is meant to be seen. The plan depends on Israel being visible while the ambush stays hidden.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the narrative’s care with geography, which grounds the account in real places and real movements. God’s acts in history are concrete, not abstract. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the vivid, step-by-step account of the battle, and neither finds a theological dispute in it.

verses.text: He took about five thousand men, and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, on the west side of the city.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua sets “about five thousand men” in ambush “between Bethel and Ai, on the west side of the city.” Arminian readers note the difference from the thirty thousand of 8:3, and observe that interpreters handle it in different ways. The text does not explain the relation, and it is best to acknowledge the question honestly rather than force a solution.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the difficulty, noting that proposals include two distinct forces, a summary followed by detail, or a different sense of the numbers. Scripture’s reliability does not depend on resolving every such question. Shared ground: both traditions treat the issue with humility and focus on the narrative’s clear point, that Israel follows God’s plan.

verses.text: So they set the people, even all the army who was on the north of the city, and their ambush on the west of the city; and Joshua went that night into the middle of the valley.
verses.arminianNotes: The army is set “on the north of the city” and the ambush “on the west,” and Joshua goes “that night into the middle of the valley.” Arminian readers note Joshua’s willingness to place himself in a visible, exposed position as part of the plan, leading by example.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the positioning of the forces sets the stage for God’s promised victory. Each detail serves the purpose God announced in 8:1. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a narrative step that heightens suspense and shows Joshua’s courageous obedience.

verses.text: When the king of Ai saw it, they hurried and rose up early, and the men of the city went out against Israel to battle, he and all his people, at the time appointed, before the Arabah; but he didn’t know that there was an ambush against him behind the city.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Ai hurries out early “at the time appointed, before the Arabah,” but “he didn’t know that there was an ambush against him behind the city.” Arminian readers note the dramatic irony: the king acts freely and confidently, but without knowledge of what has been prepared against him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the king’s ignorance a picture of how God’s purposes unfold through the free actions of people who do not know them. The phrase “at the time appointed” adds a sense of things moving to their set end. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as dramatic irony and see the king’s overconfidence as mirroring Israel’s own failure in chapter 7.

verses.text: Joshua and all Israel made as if they were beaten before them, and fled by the way of the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua and all Israel make “as if they were beaten before them” and flee “by the way of the wilderness.” Arminian readers note that the same image of flight that marked Israel’s defeat in 7:4–5 now becomes a deliberate strategy. What once was humiliation is now obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Israel’s apparent weakness is the means of victory, a pattern that recurs in Scripture, where God works through what looks like defeat. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the reversal of chapter 7, and both treat the feigned retreat as an ordinary military tactic within the narrative.

verses.text: All the people who were in the city were called together to pursue after them. They pursued Joshua, and were drawn away from the city.
verses.arminianNotes: All the people in the city are “called together to pursue,” and they are “drawn away from the city.” Arminian readers note how fully the enemy commits to the chase, leaving the city exposed. Overconfidence leads them into the very trap Joshua described in 8:6.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Joshua’s words in 8:6 fulfilled exactly, confirming that the plan given under God’s direction is unfolding as intended. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the turning point of the battle, where the enemy’s confidence and the city’s defenselessness set up the victory of 8:18–29.

verses.text: There was not a man left in Ai or Bethel who didn’t go out after Israel. They left the city open, and pursued Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: “There was not a man left in Ai or Bethel who didn’t go out after Israel.” They leave the city open. Arminian readers note that the mention of Bethel shows the defenders of neighboring towns joining in the pursuit, leaving both exposed through their own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how completely the plan works, as every defender is drawn out and the city left open for the ambush. God’s promise in 8:1 is about to be fulfilled. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the setup of the ambush, and neither finds a doctrinal contrast in it.
